text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementPhysicsThe Everlasting Life of Maxwell’s DemonHow the great scientist’s thought experiment in the 19th century, which reconciled God and physics, remains vital in science todayPBBy Philip Ball9:00 AM CST on November 19, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleJames Clerk Maxwell had good reason to feel contented in 1867. That year the Scottish physicist explained how the properties of gases derive from the frenetic motions of their inscrutable molecular particles. Two years earlier he had published a theory that united electricity and magnetism, one of the supreme achievements of 19th-century science, and a foundational law of physics. Maxwell had even made the first-ever proper color photograph. He was arguably the most distinguished physical scientist in Great Britain. But something deep in the laws of physics was troubling him. To get around it, Maxwell enlisted the help of a demon.The problem was the second law of thermodynamics. It was inferred in the mid-19th century by the German physicist Rudolf Clausius. In Clausius’s formulation, the second law insisted that heat can never spontaneously pass from a cold substance to a hotter one. This is what we know intuitively: Hot coffee always cools, but cold coffee never spontaneously gets hot again.This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from Nautilus.To get it in print, join by Nov 30.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
